title: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning
pub: US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, No. 22-12581
author: US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit · Kevin C. Newsom

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Insurance interpretation: Coverage turned on application wording
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: the court affirmed coverage-related rulings based on Snell’s insurance application and controlling Alabama law, without needing to resolve the ordinary meaning of “landscaping.” It also confirms that Newsom’s separate interpretive discussion was distinct from the holding and that the supplied material does not establish a substantive LLM proposal.
qs: Even taking the term “landscaping” as ambiguous,         construing it in Snell’s favor, and applying Alabama law’s broad         understanding of the causal term “arises out of,” Snell’s claim still         fails.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: Newsom supports the core proposition that LLM outputs should not be relied on without scrutiny. His prediction that hallucinations will decline and his view that risk varies by task qualify, but do not reject, the need for verification; he also reinforces the cluster’s broader concern about representativeness.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The concurrence strongly aligns with selective, human-led deployment: it confines LLMs to a bounded interpretive-assistance role, rejects mechanistic reliance, and stresses verification, contextual judgment, careful query design and transparency. Its predictions about improving models do not displace that overall position.

kp.k: LLMs warrant consideration as supplementary interpretive tools
kp.d: In his May 28, 2024 concurrence, Judge Newsom tentatively proposes exploring whether LLMs can assist judges and lawyers in determining the ordinary meaning of legal texts. His proposal concerns an additional interpretive resource, not a replacement for dictionaries, semantic canons or judicial judgment, and is not a holding adopting AI-based interpretation.
qs: Might LLMs be useful in the interpretation of legal texts?
Having initially thought the idea positively ludicrous, I think I’m now a pretty firm “maybe.”

kp.k: The experiment did not determine the court’s judgment
kp.d: Newsom consulted ChatGPT and Google’s Bard while considering whether installing an in-ground trampoline constituted landscaping. ChatGPT said it could; Bard offered a more qualified answer. These exchanges are an account of exploratory judicial research, not a systematic evaluation. The court ultimately resolved coverage through Snell’s insurance application under Alabama law, without needing to decide the disputed ordinary meaning.
qs: Yes, installing an in-ground trampoline can be considered a part of landscaping.
Bard was more equivocal than ChatGPT had been.
We conclude we need not resolve those issues here.

kp.k: Training data may illuminate ordinary language in context
kp.d: Newsom argues that broad language-training datasets and contextual language prediction may make LLMs useful for ordinary-meaning analysis. Citing Engel and McAdams, he reports that GPT-3.5 Turbo trained on between 400 and 500 billion words. He characterizes outputs as probabilistic predictions, acknowledges uncertainty about training-data composition, and does not establish their interpretive accuracy through testing.
qs: LLMs train on ordinary-language inputs.
LLMs can “understand” context.
To be clear, I do mean “predictions.”
I’ll confess to a bit of uncertainty about exactly what data LLMs use for training.

kp.k: Accessibility could broaden participation in legal interpretation
kp.d: Newsom suggests that accessible LLMs could give judges, lawyers, litigants and ordinary citizens an inexpensive interpretive research resource. He contrasts their availability with the practical burdens of widespread citizen surveys and the costs of paid dictionaries and legal-research subscriptions. His expectations about falling relative costs and open-source performance are prospective, not demonstrated market findings.
qs: LLMs are readily accessible (and increasingly so) to judges, lawyers, and, perhaps most importantly, ordinary citizens.
Second, it provides judges, lawyers, and litigants an inexpensive research tool.
judges and lawyers have neither the time nor the resources to poll ordinary citizens on a widespread basis.

kp.d: Newsom recommends disclosing prompts and responses, as he does in the concurrence’s appendix. He argues that this may make interpretive research more transparent than selecting dictionary definitions without explaining the selection process. He nevertheless acknowledges proprietary training data and imperfect knowledge of LLM construction; his transparency claim is comparative and qualified.
qs: full disclosure of both the queries put to the LLMs (imperfect as mine might have been) and the models’ answers.
the choice among dictionary definitions involves a measure of discretion

kp.k: Hallucinations require caution rather than blind reliance
kp.d: Newsom identifies fabricated output, including nonexistent case citations, as a serious objection. He speculates that technological improvement will reduce hallucinations and that general meaning questions may be less vulnerable than questions with specific factual answers. These are his expectations, not measured error-rate findings. He argues against unquestioning reliance and compares the need for scrutiny with judicial scrutiny of lawyers’ representations.
qs: To me, this is among the most serious objections to using LLMs in the search for ordinary meaning.
there’s every reason to believe that hallucinations will become fewer and farther between.
the “hallucination” problem counsels against blind-faith reliance on LLM outputs

kp.k: Offline and regional usage may be underrepresented
kp.d: Newsom warns that internet-based training may inadequately represent poorer communities, potentially disproportionately minorities and rural populations, as well as speech that never becomes digitized. His example is ChatGPT’s sled-only explanation of “toboggan,” which omitted the Southern and Midland stocking-cap sense. He recommends broader, more representative data and context-sensitive queries, while treating the limitations as serious but not necessarily fatal.
qs: the risk that certain communities’ word-usage outputs aren’t adequately reflected in LLMs’ training-data inputs is real
it responded with only the first, sled-based explanation.
more data, from more sources, representing a more representative cross-section of Americans.

kp.k: Strategic prompting and training-data manipulation pose risks
kp.d: Newsom considers whether lawyers and judges could shop among models or manipulate prompts to obtain preferred interpretations, and whether prospective litigants—including AI companies—could corrupt training inputs. He views these as genuine concerns but argues that disclosure, training cutoffs, dataset scale and querying multiple models may constrain them. These proposed protections are reasoned assessments rather than tested safeguards.
qs: shopping around among the available models or manipulating queries.
the same AI companies that have developed and are training the LLMs might themselves be litigants.
that risk, it seems to me, could be mitigated, if not eliminated, by querying multiple models rather than just one.

kp.k: Human judgment must retain responsibility for applying law
kp.d: Newsom expressly rejects mechanistically applying an LLM’s definition to case facts and rendering judgment. Reflecting on his own experiment, he identifies general meaning questions as more appropriate than asking a model whether specific conduct falls within the term. His proposed division of work leaves application and decision-making with the human interpreter.
qs: The models’ highest and best use is (like a dictionary) helping to discern how normal people use and understand language, not in applying a particular meaning to a particular set of facts to suggest an answer to a particular question.

kp.k: Interpretive methods need robustness and temporal controls
kp.d: Newsom recommends trying and reporting different prompts, disclosing the range of responses, and consulting multiple models. Reporting suggestions from scholarship, he discusses requesting confidence levels or repeating questions and recording response frequencies to reflect probabilistic outputs. He also calls for the ability to restrict queries to relevant historical periods: the policy here dated to 2017, but other interpretive disputes concern meanings in 1787, 1868 or 1964. These are methodological proposals, not validated procedures.
qs: the models can be sensitive to prompts and that the results can vary accordingly.
some who have considered how LLMs might be used to interpret contracts have suggested that users seek not just answers but also “confidence” levels.
it would be enormously helpful—if it’s not already possible—for AI engineers to devise a way in which queries could be limited to particular timeframes.

pts.k: Judge Kevin C. Newsom proposes LLMs as supplementary tools for interpreting ordinary meaning, not substitutes for judicial judgment.
pts.d: In his concurrence, Newsom tentatively argues that models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude may supply useful information about ordinary language when interpreting legal instruments. He attributes this potential to broad language-training inputs and contextual language prediction. He also claims that accessible LLMs could make interpretive research cheaper and more widely available, and that disclosure of prompts and responses could improve transparency relative to existing dictionary-based practice. He regards LLM research as potentially more practical than citizen surveys and less susceptible to some discretionary input-selection problems associated with corpus methods. These are proposals and comparative assessments, not findings adopted by the court. He predicts continued growth in LLM use and fewer hallucinations as technology improves, without specifying a timetable or measured improvement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Newsom’s exploratory experience in this case, supplemented by scholarship and comparisons with existing interpretive tools.
pts.d: Newsom describes difficulty applying dictionary definitions of landscaping, followed by queries to ChatGPT and Google’s Bard about the word’s ordinary meaning and whether installing an in-ground trampoline qualifies. The appendix reproduces the questions and answers: ChatGPT said installation could qualify, while Bard distinguished broad and narrow definitions. Newsom considered these answers informative but acknowledged the danger of accepting an answer because it matched his prior impressions. His queries cost nothing. He cites Arbel and Hoffman and Engel and McAdams concerning generative interpretation, training scale, prompting and repeated querying, alongside literature on dictionaries, surveys and corpus linguistics. He also acknowledges uncertainty about training-data composition and cites a reported fabricated-citation incident as evidence of hallucination risk. The concurrence supplies neither a controlled accuracy study nor measured cost savings. The court resolved the insurance dispute through the application’s disclaimer, so the LLM exploration was not necessary to the judgment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The May 2024 proposal concerns cautious present experimentation, with broader usefulness conditional on safeguards and further technical development.
pts.d: Newsom offers preliminary views rather than a deployment schedule. He limits the proposed use to assistance with ordinary meaning, leaving technical or specialized meanings aside. He favors general language questions rather than asking models to apply a definition to facts and decide a dispute. Suggested safeguards include disclosing prompts and the range of answers, varying prompts, consulting multiple models, and exploring confidence outputs or repeated responses. He identifies hallucination, incomplete representation of offline speech, regional usage, strategic prompting and possible training-data manipulation as risks. Historical interpretation presents a further condition: outputs must reflect meaning when the legal text was adopted. The policy here dated from 2017, but more distant historical usage may require time-limited queries or other engineering improvements whose availability he does not establish.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Judges, lawyers, litigants and citizens could gain an inexpensive interpretive aid, while underrepresented communities risk having their language usages inadequately reflected.
pts.d: Newsom identifies judges and lawyers as prospective users of an additional research tool, with ordinary citizens also potentially gaining direct access to interpretive assistance. His democratization claim concerns access to interpretation, not demonstrated reductions in unmet civil legal need. Judicial responsibility remains human. Poorer communities, potentially including disproportionate numbers of minorities and rural residents, may be disadvantaged if their usages are missing from online training sources. Academics and AI engineers are invited to improve representativeness, transparency and methods. The concurrence makes no concrete prediction about law-firm staffing, lawyer displacement, billing models or legal-market shares.
